# Observation models and simulated data {#sec-observation-models}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Self-study**: not taught at the workshop, but complete and ready to use on your own.
:::

## Learning goals

Every earlier chapter built a *process model*: a set of rules that generate the
latent trajectory of an epidemic. Data, however, are never the latent process.
They are noisy, incomplete counts produced by surveillance systems. This chapter
separates the two ideas explicitly and shows how to attach an **observation
model** to a deterministic SIR process so that we can simulate realistic case
reports. After working through it you should be able to

- distinguish a process model from an observation model, and explain why
  fitting a model to case reports requires stating both. This is what you must
  be able to state before anyone can fit anything, and it is where
  @sec-parameter-estimation and
  @sec-bayesian-inference begin;
- derive daily incidence from a cumulative-infection state and express it as the
  mean of a count distribution;
- implement Poisson and negative-binomial observation models in Julia with
  reproducible random streams; and
- reason about reporting fraction, overdispersion, and the limits of the
  independence assumptions baked into these models.

## Model assumptions and classification

The process model is the standard homogeneously mixing SIR model of
@kermack1927, augmented with a cumulative-incidence state $C$. We reuse the
baseline course scenario throughout: $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$,
$N=1000$, contact rate $c=10$, transmission probability $\beta=0.05$, and
recovery rate $\gamma=0.25$, giving a basic reproduction number
$R_0 = \beta c / \gamma = 2$.

| Aspect | Process model | Observation model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Determinism | deterministic | stochastic |
| Time | continuous | discrete (daily) |
| State | continuous ($S,I,R,C \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$) | discrete counts ($Y_t \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$) |
| Representation | population counts, $S+I+R=N$ | reported cases |

The observation model rests on three assumptions. First, only *new* infections
generate case reports, so the relevant signal is incidence, not prevalence.
Second, each latent case is reported independently with probability $\rho$ (the
reporting fraction). Third, conditional on the latent incidence, the counts on
different days are independent.

The second assumption on its own does not give a Poisson count, and it is worth
being exact about why. If day $t$ contained a *known whole number* $n_t$ of
infections and each were reported independently with probability $\rho$, the
count would be $\operatorname{Binomial}(n_t, \rho)$, whose variance
$n_t\rho(1-\rho)$ is smaller than its mean. What the deterministic process
supplies is not a whole number: $x_t$ is an expected incidence, a real-valued
intensity. The standard reading is therefore that the latent count is itself
$\operatorname{Poisson}(x_t)$ around that intensity, and independent reporting
thins it. Thinning a Poisson variable is exactly Poisson, so

$$
N_t \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(x_t), \quad
Y_t \mid N_t \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(N_t, \rho)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Y_t \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\rho\, x_t),
$$

with no approximation. This is the justification used throughout the chapter:
the Poisson model absorbs both the randomness of who gets infected and the
randomness of who gets reported. Relaxing the independence of individual
reports, so that cases arrive in correlated batches, motivates the
negative-binomial extension.

## Equations

The process model integrates

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\beta c \frac{S I}{N}, &
\frac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \beta c \frac{S I}{N} - \gamma I, \\[2pt]
\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \gamma I, &
\frac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \beta c \frac{S I}{N},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sir-cumulative}

where $C(t)$ accumulates infections but never decreases. The **latent
incidence** over day $t$ is the increment of $C$,

$$
x_t = C(t) - C(t-1) = \int_{t-1}^{t} \beta c \frac{S(\tau) I(\tau)}{N}\,\mathrm{d}\tau .
$$ {#eq-incidence}

By the thinning argument above, a Poisson latent count observed with reporting
probability $\rho$ stays Poisson, with its mean scaled to the reported fraction
of latent incidence,

$$
Y_t \mid x_t \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(\rho\, x_t), \qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \operatorname{Var}[Y_t] = \rho\, x_t .
$$ {#eq-poisson}

Poisson counts are *equidispersed*: the variance equals the mean. Real
surveillance data are usually **overdispersed**. The negative-binomial model
adds a dispersion parameter $r>0$,

$$
Y_t \mid x_t \sim \operatorname{NegBin}\!\big(r, \tfrac{r}{r + \rho x_t}\big),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y_t] = \rho x_t, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y_t] = \rho x_t + \frac{(\rho x_t)^2}{r},
$$ {#eq-negbin}

so the variance exceeds the mean by $(\rho x_t)^2 / r$, and the Poisson model is
recovered as $r \to \infty$.

## Julia implementation

The process kernel `sir_cumulative_ode!` and the reproducible data generator
`synthetic_incidence` are provided by the course package `EpiModelingCourse`.
The chapter and its slides both integrate the packaged kernel, and the companion
notebook additionally uses `synthetic_incidence`, which wraps the same solve and
returns a fixed-schema `DataFrame`; the worksheet deliberately writes its own
four-line copy so that it can be read without the package. We
solve the process model with [OrdinaryDiffEq.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/OrdinaryDiffEq/stable/),
draw observations with [Distributions.jl](https://juliastats.org/Distributions.jl/stable/),
and keep randomness reproducible with
[StableRNGs.jl](https://github.com/JuliaRandom/StableRNGs.jl).

```{julia}
#| label: setup
#| output: false
using EpiModelingCourse
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using DelayDiffEq
using DiffEqCallbacks
using Distributions
using StableRNGs
using CairoMakie

CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
set_theme!(course_theme())
palette = course_palette()
```

### The latent process

We integrate @eq-sir-cumulative over 40 days with the baseline parameters and
extract daily incidence by differencing $C$ (Method 1). Because the only exit
from $S$ is infection, cumulative incidence must equal susceptible depletion,
$C(t) = S(0) - S(t)$, which we will use as a validation check.

```{julia}
#| label: process
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0]      # S, I, R, C
p = BASELINE_PARAMETERS            # β = 0.05, c = 10, γ = 0.25, N = 1000
tspan = (0.0, 40.0)
obstimes = 1.0:1.0:40.0

prob = ODEProblem(sir_cumulative_ode!, u0, tspan, p)
sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)

cumulative = Array(sol)[4, :]
incidence = cumulative[2:end] .- cumulative[1:(end - 1)]   # latent xₜ
```

### Poisson and negative-binomial observations

With the latent incidence in hand, the observation model is just a draw from a
count distribution. We use a full reporting fraction ($\rho = 1$) here so that
the observation noise, rather than under-reporting, is isolated. Each
observation model gets its own `StableRNG` so the streams are independent and
reproducible.

```{julia}
#| label: observations
reporting_fraction = 1.0
expected = reporting_fraction .* incidence

poisson_obs = rand.(StableRNG(20240607), Poisson.(expected))

# NegativeBinomial(r, p) with mean μ uses p = r / (r + μ); r sets dispersion.
dispersion = 10.0
nb(μ, r) = NegativeBinomial(r, r / (r + μ))
negbin_rng = StableRNG(20240608)
negbin_obs = [rand(negbin_rng, nb(μ, dispersion)) for μ in expected]

(total_latent = round(sum(expected); digits = 1),
 total_poisson = sum(poisson_obs),
 total_negbin = sum(negbin_obs))
```

The obvious next step is to take the variance of `poisson_obs` across the forty
days, compare it with their mean, and declare the Poisson model equidispersed.
That comparison is invalid, and the reason is worth more than the check would
have been. The forty draws do not share a mean: $\mu_t$ climbs and falls with the
epidemic. For independent $Y_t\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_t)$, the across-day
sample variance estimates

$$
\mathbb{E}[s_Y^2] = \bar\mu + s_\mu^2,
$$ {#eq-variance-decomposition}

the average Poisson variance *plus* the variance of the means themselves. Here
the second term dominates, so the across-day variance comes out at roughly twelve
times the mean. Nothing is wrong with the model; the statistic simply measures
the epidemic curve rather than the observation noise.

Dispersion is a statement about a single day, so it has to be measured with
replicate draws at a fixed day.

```{julia}
#| label: dispersion
peak = argmax(expected)
peak_rng = StableRNG(20240609)
poisson_peak = [rand(peak_rng, Poisson(expected[peak])) for _ in 1:4000]
negbin_peak = [rand(peak_rng, nb(expected[peak], dispersion)) for _ in 1:4000]

(across_day_variance = round(var(poisson_obs); digits = 1),
 decomposition = round(mean(expected) + var(expected); digits = 1),
 peak_mean = round(expected[peak]; digits = 1),
 poisson_ratio = round(var(poisson_peak) / mean(poisson_peak); digits = 2),
 negbin_ratio = round(var(negbin_peak) / mean(negbin_peak); digits = 2),
 negbin_predicted = round(1 + expected[peak] / dispersion; digits = 2))
```

The across-day variance matches @eq-variance-decomposition rather than the mean,
which confirms the diagnosis. At the peak day the replicate Poisson counts have a
variance-to-mean ratio near one, as @eq-poisson requires, while the
negative-binomial counts sit near the $1 + \mu_t/r$ predicted by @eq-negbin. The
same trap is worth remembering when reading real data: an overdispersed-looking
case series may only be an epidemic curve.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-observations
#| fig-cap: "Latent daily incidence (line) with one realisation of Poisson (left) and overdispersed negative-binomial (right) case reports. Both share the same latent mean; the negative-binomial scatter is wider."
fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Time (days)", ylabel = "New cases per day",
    title = "Poisson observations")
barplot!(ax1, obstimes, poisson_obs; color = (palette.incidence, 0.5))
lines!(ax1, obstimes, incidence; color = palette.infected, linewidth = 3,
    label = "Latent incidence")
axislegend(ax1; position = :rt)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "Time (days)", ylabel = "New cases per day",
    title = "Negative-binomial observations (r = $(Int(dispersion)))")
barplot!(ax2, obstimes, negbin_obs; color = (palette.incidence, 0.5))
lines!(ax2, obstimes, incidence; color = palette.infected, linewidth = 3)
fig
```

### Alternative ways to obtain daily incidence

Differencing the cumulative state (Method 1) is the most robust route, but two
other constructions appear in practice. A [PresetTimeCallback](https://docs.sciml.ai/DiffEqCallbacks/stable/)
can reset $C$ to zero at each observation time so that the saved value *is* the
daily increment (Method 2). A delay differential equation solved with
[DelayDiffEq.jl](https://github.com/SciML/DelayDiffEq.jl) can track a sliding
one-day window directly (Method 3). We implement both to compare them against
Method 1.

Method 3 is a cross-check, not something you need to be able to write. Its
machinery (a history function `h(p, t)` supplying the state before the
simulation began, `constant_lags`, and the `MethodOfSteps` solver) is developed
in the [delay differential equations
appendix](../appendices/01-delay-differential-equations.html); read the block
below for what it computes rather than for how it is assembled.

```{julia}
#| label: alt-methods
# Method 2: reset the cumulative counter at each observation time.
# `save_positions = (true, false)` keeps the value *before* each reset and drops
# the zero after it. Without it the solution stores both at the same time point,
# and reading the second one returns the reset value instead of the day's count.
reset_C!(integrator) = integrator.u[4] = 0.0
cb = PresetTimeCallback(collect(obstimes), reset_C!;
    save_positions = (true, false))
sol_cb = solve(prob, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0, callback = cb,
    abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
incidence_cb = sol_cb(obstimes)[4, :]

# Method 3: a sliding-window delay differential equation for daily incidence.
function sir_window_dde!(du, u, h, p, t)
    S, I, R, C = u
    N = p.N
    infection = p.β * p.c * S * I / N
    recovery = p.γ * I
    past = h(p, t - 1.0)          # state one day earlier
    past_infection = p.β * p.c * past[1] * past[2] / N
    du[1] = -infection
    du[2] = infection - recovery
    du[3] = recovery
    du[4] = infection - past_infection
    return nothing
end
history(p, t) = zeros(4)
prob_dde = DDEProblem(sir_window_dde!, u0, history, tspan, p; constant_lags = [1.0])
sol_dde = solve(prob_dde, MethodOfSteps(Tsit5());
    abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
incidence_dde = sol_dde(obstimes)[4, :]

(method2_max_gap = maximum(abs.(incidence_cb .- incidence)),
 method3_max_gap = maximum(abs.(incidence_dde .- incidence)))
```

All three agree to solver tolerance, and they must: the three constructions are
the same quantity written three ways. Method 3 makes that easiest to see. With
the zero prehistory above, the infection rate $q(s)$ vanishes for $s<0$, so

$$
C_w(t) = \int_0^t \big[q(s) - q(s-1)\big]\,\mathrm{d}s
       = \int_0^t q - \int_0^{t-1} q
       = \int_{t-1}^{t} q \quad (t \ge 1),
$$

which is exactly $C(t) - C(t-1)$, the increment Method 1 differences. Any
remaining gap is numerical, not conceptual, and it is dominated by solver
tolerances: with the delay equation left at the default tolerances rather than
the $10^{-10}$ used here, the discrepancy grows by roughly six orders of
magnitude while remaining a numerical artefact throughout.

Method 1 is still the one to prefer downstream, but for practical reasons rather
than mathematical ones: it needs no callback, no history function and no delay
solver, and it cannot be broken by reading the state on the wrong side of a
discontinuity.

## Validation

We check three structural properties. First, conservation: cumulative incidence
must equal susceptible depletion. Second, non-negativity: sampled counts are
never negative. Third, the law of large numbers: averaging many independent
Poisson realisations must converge to the latent mean @eq-poisson.

```{julia}
#| label: validation
S = Array(sol)[1, :]
conservation_error = maximum(abs.(cumulative .- (990.0 .- S)))

replicates = [rand.(StableRNG(seed), Poisson.(expected)) for seed in 1:2000]
mc_mean = reduce(+, replicates) ./ length(replicates)
lln_error = maximum(abs.(mc_mean .- expected))

(conservation_error = conservation_error,
 counts_nonnegative = all(poisson_obs .>= 0) && all(negbin_obs .>= 0),
 lln_error = lln_error)
```

The conservation error sits at the level of the ODE tolerances, all counts are
non-negative, and the Monte Carlo mean of 2000 Poisson realisations reproduces
the latent incidence to within a fraction of a case.

## Interpretation and limitations

The observation model is deliberately simple, and each assumption is a modelling
choice a practitioner must defend. Lowering either $\rho$ or $\beta$ pulls the
expected counts down, so a small epidemic reported fully and a large epidemic
reported partially produce case series of similar size. But halving $\rho$ and
doubling $\beta$ is not the same epidemic, because changing $\beta$ also moves
the peak *day*, and that timing information is what a fit has to work with.

Whether the timing information establishes structural identifiability is not an
open question under the assumptions used here: with $N$, the initial state, $c$
and $\gamma$ fixed, and reporting constant and instantaneous, $\rho$ and $\beta$
are not interchangeable. Changing $\rho$ rescales the expected series, whereas
changing $\beta$ also changes its growth, timing and shape. Whether a finite,
noisy series estimates them precisely is a separate question of practical
identifiability. Uncertainty in the initial state can flatten the likelihood into
a ridge; an unknown population size can be confounded with the reporting
fraction; and a sufficiently flexible time-varying reporting fraction can make
$\beta$ structurally non-identifiable. Each relaxation therefore requires its own
identifiability analysis, of the kind taken up in
@sec-sensitivity-and-identifiability.

The Poisson model forces variance to equal the mean, and real case series are
usually more variable than that. The negative-binomial model in @eq-negbin is
the usual remedy, at the cost of one extra parameter, but it is worth being
precise about what that buys: it widens the *marginal* distribution of each
day's count, and does nothing else. It does not explain why the counts are
overdispersed, and it cannot represent a mechanism that acts across days.
Batched reporting, day-of-week effects and drifting reporting effort all
correlate neighbouring days, and a per-day variance leaves that structure
untouched. Super-spreading is not a reporting phenomenon at all: it is variation
in transmission, and belongs in the process model, where the stochastic
formulations of @sec-jump-processes place it.

Two mechanisms are missing rather than approximated. The first is reporting
delay. We assumed every infection is notified on the day it occurs, whereas real
systems notify days to weeks later, and a delay model distributes each day's
infections forward over a range of later reporting dates, so that a single day's
count mixes several days of infections. Method 3 does not do this: its window is
a trailing one, and the derivation above shows it returns exactly $C(t)-C(t-1)$,
the same day's incidence rather than a lagged or smeared version of it. Nothing
in this chapter represents notification delay. The second is the day-of-week
artefact, which conditional independence across days rules out by construction.
The two are distinct mechanisms with distinct remedies, and operational
nowcasting systems estimate them separately.

These simulated datasets are nonetheless the raw material for inference:
@sec-parameter-estimation estimates
parameters from them by maximum likelihood, and
@sec-bayesian-inference does so with Bayesian methods. Both are
self-study chapters rather than workshop sessions; the workshop programme points
instead at an external course dedicated to model fitting and inference.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch08-ex1}

Using the baseline scenario and Method 1, generate case reports under a partial
reporting fraction $\rho = 0.4$ with the Poisson observation model. Plot the
latent incidence and the reported counts on the same axes, and compute the total
number of latent versus reported cases over the 40 days. Explain why the reported
peak looks like a smaller epidemic. Then test how far that resemblance goes:
find the $\beta$ that reproduces the same peak *height* under full reporting, and
compare that series with the reported one. Which features of the curve still tell
the two scenarios apart, and what else would you need to know to rely on them?

### Exercise 2 {#ch08-ex2}

Fix the mean of the negative-binomial observation model to the latent incidence
and vary the dispersion parameter over $r \in \{1, 5, 50, 500\}$. For each
value, draw 1000 replicate time series and estimate the ratio of the sample
variance to the sample mean at the epidemic peak. Check each estimate against
the ratio $1 + \mu_{\text{peak}}/r$ implied by @eq-negbin, and comment on how
slowly that ratio decreases toward 1: the peak mean is close to 45 cases, so
$r = 50$ still leaves the variance nearly twice the mean, and only $r = 500$
comes near equidispersion.
